The Indus Valley Civilization. One of the world's three great ancient urban societies, flourishing roughly three thousand three hundred to thirteen hundred BCE alongside Egypt and Mesopotamia. It developed along the Indus River and its tributaries in what is now Pakistan and India, featuring planned cities, sophisticated drainage systems, and a script that scholars still cannot read.

The civilization emerged around three thousand three hundred BCE and thrived during the Mature Harappan period from twenty-six hundred to nineteen hundred BCE, then declined, possibly because of climate change or shifts in the river itself. Cities like Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were laid out on a grid with standardized brick sizes, suggesting centralized planning and authority. Streets maintained uniform widths, revealing a level of urban planning sophistication. The people developed sophisticated drainage and sanitation systems with underground pipes, flush toilets, and public baths that rivaled or even exceeded the hygiene standards of later civilizations for centuries. Wastewater flowed away from settlements through buried drains.

The Indus civilization created a pictographic script containing about four hundred symbols. It appears on seals and pottery but offers no window into their language or beliefs. Decipherment has frustrated scholars for over a century. The economic system shows evidence of extensive trade networks reaching Mesopotamia, the Arabian Peninsula, and Central Asia. Weights and measures were standardized, indicating mercantile sophistication. Seals found in Mesopotamia testify to long-distance contact. Society appears to have been egalitarian or meritocratic, with few signs of huge palaces, temples, or elite tombs. Wealth was more evenly distributed than in Egypt or Mesopotamia. The civilization disappeared around thirteen hundred BCE, and reasons remain debated. Climate change, flooding, or conquest may have led to collapse and dispersal.

Unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia, the Indus civilization left no monumental palaces, royal tombs, or temple complexes. Some archaeologists infer a more egalitarian society or a theocratic system without hereditary rulers. The decentralized nature of Indus sites, with no evidence of a single capital or dominant center, suggests distributed political authority, possibly organized as city-states or a confederation. The largest developed city, Mohenjo-daro, was excavated extensively in the early twentieth century. The Indus River itself provided the flooding and fertility that supported this civilization and shaped its seasonal cycles. Most Indus Valley sites are located in modern Pakistan, with Mohenjo-daro now a UNESCO World Heritage site, while some sites lie in modern India and may have influenced later Indian civilization. The civilization was contemporaneous with Bronze Age societies in Mesopotamia and Egypt, and Indus sites remain prime examples of how archaeology reveals the urban complexity of ancient civilizations.
